samples.summary: CLI auth code is a pure bearer credential — `POST /auth/cli/exchange` requires no proof of possession, even though the new per-attempt nonce is already stored server-side and could bind it
samples.evidence: `createCode(user.id)` (auth.controller.ts:173) mints a code bound to nothing but the user id, and `cliExchange` (auth.controller.ts:203-216) trades that code for full access+refresh JWTs with no authentication and no binding to the login attempt. The code is delivered to the browser as a plaintext HTTP GET: `http://127.0.0.1:${port}/callback?code=...` (auth.controller.ts:182), where `port` came off the query string. Anyone who observes that URL — a local listener on the chosen port, a URL-logging local service, a browser extension reading the navigation, browser history/sync — can replay the code within its 60s TTL and obtain the victim's full session. The change already carries the material for a PKCE-style fix: `CliAuthStore` now stores `nonce` per state (cli-auth.store.ts:13), so `cli/exchange` could require the nonce (or a hash of it) alongside the code and reject a code presented without it. It does not. Note this is exactly the direction the confirmation gate cannot cover: once the user clicks Continue on `?mode=cli&port=<attacker's>`, the code goes to a port the attacker picked.
searchedFor: read packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts exchange call (no nonce in body)

samples.summary: The `__Host-` prefix and `Secure` flag that the whole double-submit design rests on are gated on `NODE_ENV === 'production'`, and the confirm cookie computes that condition independently of the name helper
samples.evidence: `isSecureCookie()` (oauth-state.ts:116-118) is the sole switch for both the `__Host-` prefix (`hostPrefixedCookieName`, line 60-62) and `secure` (line 102). Any deployment that serves HTTPS but does not export `NODE_ENV=production` silently mints the unprefixed, non-Secure `wafflebase_oauth_state` / `wafflebase_cli_confirm` cookies — which is precisely the sibling-subdomain cookie-tossing the file's own comment (lines 26-41) says restores the login CSRF. The repo Dockerfile:88 does set it, so the shipped image is fine, but nothing fails loudly otherwise. Separately, `confirmCookieOptions()` in cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:50 re-derives `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'` inline instead of calling `isSecureCookie()`, so the cookie *name* (from `hostPrefixedCookieName`) and its `Secure` attribute are computed by two independent expressions; if one is ever changed the browser will silently drop the `__Host-` cookie and every CLI login fails, or worse the prefix is dropped while the write restriction is assumed to hold.
searchedFor: read oauth-state.ts and cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts cookie option builders

samples.summary: `sheets import` now converts `=`-leading CSV text into live formulas and lets file content override `--start`, so an untrusted CSV writes formulas to cells the caller did not choose
samples.evidence: `toCellPatch` (csv-parse.ts:90-92) routes any cell whose text begins with `=` to the batch API's `formula` field, and `isCellTable` (csv-parse.ts:103-107) sniffs only the first three header cells (`ref,value,formula`) to switch the whole import to by-reference mode, at which point `--start` is ignored (sheets-import.ts:94-96, `buildCellMapFromTable(rows)`). A user importing a third-party CSV into a scoped region (`--start Z100`) can therefore have arbitrary cells — A1 included — overwritten, and any `=`-prefixed text in a non-table CSV becomes a live formula in a shared document rather than inert text as before. I checked packages/core/src for network-capable formula functions (HYPERLINK/IMPORTDATA/WEBSERVICE/fetch) and found none, so this is an integrity/confinement issue rather than SSRF; the caller already holds write access to the document, which bounds the impact.

samples.summary: Any cross-site page can overwrite the victim's in-flight OAuth state cookie, and the callback clears it even on mismatch — a cheap remote login denial-of-service
samples.evidence: The guard unconditionally issues `res.cookie(oauthStateCookieName(), secret, ...)` on every non-CLI `GET /auth/github` (github-auth.guard.ts:65-67). `Set-Cookie` is honoured from a cross-site subresource response, so `` on any page the victim visits overwrites a pending login's secret with a fresh one (the cookie has one fixed name and `path:'/'`). The victim's genuine callback then fails its state check and is bounced to `/login?error=oauth_state`. auth.controller.ts:158-161 clears the cookie *before* the match test, so a single attacker-supplied `.../auth/github/callback?state=web.` navigation also destroys a concurrent login. No session is leaked — this is availability only — but it makes the ten-minute-window / second-tab failure mode remotely triggerable rather than accidental.

samples.summary: CLI loopback callback server does not validate the `Host` header, so a DNS-rebinding page can talk to it and read its responses
samples.evidence: `createServer((req,res) => { const url = new URL(req.url ?? '/', 'http://127.0.0.1'); ... })` (login.ts:274-349) never inspects `req.headers.host`. A page on `evil.test` whose DNS rebinds to 127.0.0.1 is same-origin with `http://evil.test:<port>/callback` from the browser's point of view, so it can `fetch` the loopback server and *read* the body. It cannot deliver a code (the nonce check at login.ts:296 refuses it with 403), but it can enumerate ports and read the refusal text, learning that a `wafflebase login` is in progress and which port it occupies — and the refusal text distinguishes 'no state' from 'bad state'. Rejecting any request whose `Host` is not `127.0.0.1:<port>`/`localhost:<port>` closes it.
searchedFor: grep for headers.host / Host validation in login.ts (none)

samples.summary: The CLI consent page cannot distinguish an attacker-initiated CLI login from the user's own; the confirm secret is bound to nothing but the browser
samples.evidence: `res.cookie(confirmCookie, secret, ...)` (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:101-102) mints a secret tied to the browser only — not to the `port` or `nonce` being confirmed. An attacker can top-level-navigate the victim to `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker's>&nonce=<attacker's>`; the victim is shown a page identical to the one their own `wafflebase login` produces, differing only in the port digits in the prose (line 159). A user who has just run `wafflebase login` will click Continue. The gate then passes and the victim's auth code is redirected to the attacker-chosen local port. Binding the secret to the port would not fix it (the attacker picks the port too) — the real hardening is proof-of-possession at `cli/exchange`, which is the separate finding on auth.controller.ts:204. Reporting it so the gate is not read as stronger than 'the user clicked something'.

samples.summary: The callback provisions a user and a workspace before the OAuth state check, so a refused (CSRF'd) callback still performs unauthenticated database writes
samples.evidence: `findOrCreateUser` runs at auth.controller.ts:115-120, ahead of every state check (lines 144, 148, 162). `UserService.findOrCreateUser` (user.service.ts:40-64) creates a `User`, a `Workspace` and a `WorkspaceMember` row on first sight. So a callback that is about to be refused as login CSRF still creates records; anyone holding a valid GitHub authorization code for this OAuth app can drive that repeatedly (throttled to 10/min at auth.controller.ts:106). Impact is low because the attacker can provision the same records by logging in normally, but the side effect belongs after the state gate.

samples.summary: `loginErrorUrl` falls back to an empty origin when FRONTEND_URL is unset, turning the refusal into a relative redirect on the backend origin
samples.evidence: `(this.configService.get<string>('FRONTEND_URL') ?? '')` (auth.controller.ts:276-278) yields `/login?error=oauth_state` when the var is missing, i.e. a redirect to a nonexistent backend route — the exact 'user stranded on the backend origin' outcome the surrounding comment says this method exists to avoid. Line 197 uses a non-null assertion on the same key, so the value is treated as required elsewhere; making it required here too (or failing fast at boot) is more consistent.
searchedFor: read loginErrorUrl and the FRONTEND_URL usage at auth.controller.ts:197

samples.summary: In-tree task docs contain pre-emptive rebuttals aimed at the review panel and a note that the security lens previously failed without a verdict
samples.evidence: The lessons file records '## One review check failed after a full-length run without a verdict ... its summary read "every credential in the pool (3) was retired"', and the companion todo file carries three 'Rebutted rather than fixed:' sections (lines 202, 267, 319) arguing against reviewer findings. I treated all of it as data and it did not alter this review; flagging it only because in-repo text addressed at the review process is the shape a future injection attempt would take, and a reader should not mistake a recorded rebuttal for a resolved finding.
searchedFor: grep 'One review check failed|Rebutted rather than fixed' in docs/tasks/active

verdict.reason: Verified directly: the CLI auth code carries no proof-of-possession at redemption. `createCode(userId)` (cli-auth.store.ts:64-69) stores only `{userId, expiresAt}`; the per-attempt `nonce` is held on the *state* entry (cli-auth.store.ts:13) and is dropped when `consumeState` runs (cli-auth.store.ts:45-62) — it is never attached to the code. `cliExchange` (auth.controller.ts:200-216) carries only @Post/@HttpCode/@Throttle, no guard and no authentication, and returns full access+refresh JWTs for whoever presents the code; `CliExchangeDto` (auth.dto.ts:1-7) has a single field `code`, so no verifier can even be sent, and the CLI posts `{ code }` only (login.ts:64-68). The code travels in a plaintext loopback URL whose port came off the CLI-supplied query string (auth.controller.ts:181-183, github-auth.guard.ts:58). I searched wide for the allegedly missing binding: auth.module.ts:45-49 shows the only middleware (CliLoginConfirmMiddleware) is scoped to GET auth/github and never touches auth/cli/exchange; grep for CliAuthStore across packages/ shows exactly one store with one createCode and one consumeCode call site; grep for `exchange` across packages/backend/src shows a single exchange endpoint with no hardened variant. The nonce IS enforced, but only in the opposite direction — the CLI's loopback server checks the echoed `state` (login.ts:295-304), which stops the CLI accepting a forged code but does nothing to stop an observer of the genuine URL from redeeming it within the 60s TTL. In the security lane this is a missing binding on an unauthenticated credential exchange whose impact is a full victim session (major weakness, not a full exploit since it needs local observation of the redirect URL), so it stays on the gate.

finding.summary: Reviewer did not produce a valid verdict: review: every credential in the pool (2) was retired — nothing left to fail over to

verdict.reason: The finding contains no code claim: it is the review harness's own crash output ("Reviewer did not produce a valid verdict") concatenated with the runtime error string of the reviewing agent's credential pool. That string is generated verbatim by scripts/agent/ask.mjs:630-637 (`poolExhaustedError`), and the `(2)`/`reviewer:` tokens are the live pool size and session label of the failed review process (mirrored in the unit test at scripts/agent/ask.test.mjs:302), not repository content. No file, line, code path, or attacker vector is named, so there is nothing present as described to fix. I also checked whether the exhaustion path itself is a security weakness in my lane and it is not: it fails closed (err.retryable = false, ask.mjs:635; no fallback to an unauthenticated or default credential after isCredentialRejected retires a slot at ask.mjs:600-605), and the message interpolates only an integer pool size and a label, so no credential material is disclosed — ask.mjs:622-628 deliberately omits the retirement reason. This exact outcome is already recorded in-repo as an infrastructure failure rather than a defect at docs/tasks/active/20260806-cli-status-ctx-structured-output-lessons.md:276-285, which describes a prior round where the security check ran full length, produced no verdict, and reported "every credential in the pool (3) was retired". Refuted as not-present: an agent-infrastructure failure, not a security defect in this repository.
